children: Deutsche Bank submitted under 10 suspicious activity reports (SARs) to US authorities in 2019 while routing payments worth more than €20bn to Colombian lenders, the
reported, citing leaked files from an internal 2020 review code-named Project Cali.
The bank handled 171,000 payments to nine Colombian banks that year and filed no reports in Germany, despite classing Colombia as high-risk because of drug trafficking, according to
, which coordinated the investigation in Latin America. A look-back at 4,800 of the transfers generated 230 SARs.
External monitors Lee Wolosky and Dawn Smalls called the control gaps “alarming” and likened them to failings in the Epstein case, for which New York’s financial regulator had fined the bank.

Project Cali began after Germany’s BaFin ordered the lender to identify markets where it carried most correspondent flows. Deutsche found it held a 60%-80% share of euro payments in Colombia. Reviewers flagged 41 individuals and companies, including senders tied to the webcam industry, which Fenalweb estimates earns about $700mn a year. The documents do not show that investigators linked Curaçao-based Shoshoro, which sent more than $1mn to Colombia in 2019, to any specific exploitation.
Deutsche described Project Cali as “a historical review” that prompted remedial steps, and said it had cut its risk profile by dropping high-risk customers and jurisdictions.
Shares fell as much as 6.4% on November 17 after the wider leak was published,
reported, while German Finance Minister Lars Klingbeil said the lender must explain how it addressed the issues.

The case shows how concentration in correspondent banking can magnify one institution’s control gaps across a national payments system. Colombian lenders rely on such intermediaries and risk losing overseas accounts if they miss structuring, an Asobancaria representative warned in 2022, which helps explain their wariness toward the webcam sector. DANE only assigned the industry an economic activity code in August 2026. GAFILAT estimated in 2018 that cocaine-linked laundering equalled 5.4% of Colombia’s GDP.

title: Deutsche Bank’s review found gaps in controls on Colombia payments, leak shows
